reports.text: Complete study. Left ventricle normal in size with normal systolic function. Normal wall motion. The ascending aortic graft appears intact. The native aortic root is dilated. Aortic regurgitation is present. Mitral valve unremarkable. Normal right ventricular size and function. No pericardial effusion.
reports.conclusion: Intact ascending aortic graft. Dilated native aortic root. Aortic regurgitation.

documents.title: Cardiology Aortic Clinic Letter
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL — CARDIOLOGY, AORTIC CLINIC
Date of visit: 03/06/2025

Dear Colleague,

Mr. Fischer is a 28-year-old with Marfan syndrome, now four months out from emergency ascending aortic and hemiarch replacement with valve resuspension for acute type A dissection (11/2024), course complicated by a pericardial effusion requiring a window. Strong family history: father died of dissection at 42, paternal aunt with prophylactic root replacement.

He feels well and is fully active at a desk job. No chest pain, dyspnea or syncope.

Medications: metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily, lisinopril 10 mg daily, aspirin 81 mg daily.
Allergies: penicillin (rash); iodinated contrast (urticaria).

Exam: Tall, thin. Healed sternotomy. Regular rhythm, soft diastolic murmur at the right upper sternal border. Lungs clear. Radial pulses equal. No edema.

Echo today: ascending graft intact; native aortic root dilated; aortic regurgitation present; normal LV function.

Impression/plan:
1. Marfan syndrome s/p type A dissection repair with residual dilated native root. Continue beta-blocker and ACE inhibitor at current doses; BP goal is being met. Repeat aortic imaging in about a year. Given his contrast allergy, noncontrast imaging will be favored.
2. Aortic regurgitation, followed by echo.
3. Avoid heavy isometric lifting and contact sports; stimulants and decongestants should be avoided.

Thank you for allowing us to share in his care.

Cardiology

events.reason: Dyspnea and hemoptysis after cocaine inhalation

reports.text: Portable AP chest. Diffuse bilateral alveolar opacities. Postoperative sternotomy wires and mediastinal surgical changes. No pneumothorax. No large pleural effusion. Heart size within normal limits.

Flexible bronchoscopy under moderate sedation on high-flow oxygen. Airways inspected to the subsegmental level bilaterally; no endobronchial lesion and no focal bleeding source. Sequential lavage of the right middle lobe: each successive aliquot returned more hemorrhagic than the last.
reports.conclusion: Progressively hemorrhagic sequential lavage consistent with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. No endobronchial lesion.

REGIONAL HOSPITAL — EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Date of service: 07/10/2025

CC: trouble breathing, coughing blood

HPI: 29M with Marfan syndrome, s/p emergency type A dissection repair 11/2024, HTN. Friends brought him in from a party tonight; they say he inhaled something they took to be cocaine, and shortly afterward he got acutely short of breath and started bringing up blood. Arrives anxious and sweaty.

Meds: metoprolol succinate 50 daily, lisinopril 10 daily, aspirin 81 daily.
Allergies: penicillin (rash), iodinated contrast (urticaria).

Exam: BP 150/95, HR 110, RR 28, SpO2 88% on room air. Anxious, diaphoretic. Crackles in both lung fields. Healed sternotomy. Otherwise unremarkable.

Data: Hgb 13.2, WBC 12,000, plt 250,000. PT 12 sec (ref 11-13.5), PTT 30 sec (ref 25-35). D-dimer 500 ng/mL (ref <500). Urine tox positive for cocaine metabolites. Portable CXR: diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates.

MDM: Hypoxemic respiratory failure with hemoptysis and diffuse alveolar filling after inhaled cocaine; leading concern is cocaine-associated alveolar hemorrhage. Placed on high-flow nasal cannula with improvement in saturation. Aspirin held. ICU consulted.

Disposition: MICU.

documents.title: Addiction Medicine Consult
documents.author: addiction medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL — ADDICTION MEDICINE CONSULT
Date: 07/12/2025

Reason: cocaine use with life-threatening complication.

29-year-old man admitted to the ICU with alveolar hemorrhage after inhaling cocaine, on a background of Marfan syndrome and a repaired aortic dissection. Urine toxicology positive for cocaine metabolites. Interviewed at length about his cocaine use; the history meets DSM-5 criteria for stimulant use disorder, cocaine type, severe. Never smoker, drinks rarely.

Assessment: Stimulant use disorder, severe, cocaine.

Recommendations: Motivational interviewing done at bedside; he is ambivalent but engaged. No FDA-approved medication for cocaine use disorder. Recommend outpatient addiction medicine/behavioral treatment; information given. PCP to reinforce.

documents.title: ICU Discharge Summary
documents.author: critical care
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL — DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted: 07/10/2025   Discharged: 07/14/2025
Service: Medical Intensive Care

Diagnoses: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, cocaine-associated. Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, resolved. Stimulant use disorder, severe, cocaine. Marfan syndrome s/p type A dissection repair. Hypertension.

Course: Presented after inhaling cocaine with hemoptysis, hypoxemia (88% RA) and diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Managed on high-flow nasal cannula in the MICU; never required intubation. Bronchoscopy 7/11: no endobronchial lesion, sequential lavage progressively more hemorrhagic, confirming alveolar hemorrhage. ANCA and anti-GBM antibody negative. Coagulation studies normal. Hemoptysis stopped by day 2, weaned to room air on day 3. Aspirin held during the stay and resumed at discharge. Addiction medicine saw him on 7/12.

Discharge medications (unchanged from admission):
- Metoprolol succinate ER 50 mg daily
- Lisinopril 10 mg daily
- Aspirin 81 mg daily (resume)

Allergies: Penicillin (rash). Iodinated contrast (urticaria).

Follow-up: PCP within 1 week; repeat chest X-ray in 4-6 weeks; outpatient addiction treatment.
